title: Care for animals
hookLine: Jewish law forbids causing animals needless suffering

lines: A CALF RUNS TO THE RABBI.
GO, THIS IS WHAT YOU'RE FOR.
cards: A calf is being led to slaughter. It breaks away, runs to Rabbi Judah the Prince, the sage tradition credits with compiling the Mishnah, hides its head in his clothes, and cries. The rabbi says to it: go.
This is what you were created for. The Talmud says that because he showed no pity, he suffered years of illness. Then one day his housekeeper was sweeping out some baby weasels, and he stopped her.

teach.b: He told her to leave them alone, quoting a psalm: "His tender mercies are over all His works." Because he showed mercy, the Talmud says, his suffering ended.
That story sits at the heart of a principle in Jewish law called tza'ar ba'alei chayim, the suffering of living creatures: you may not cause an animal needless pain.
The Talmud debates whether the rule comes straight from the Torah or from the rabbis, and later authorities argue both ways. Look how many of the Torah's laws protect animals.

teach.h: RELEASE THE DONKEY, EVEN AN ENEMY'S.
teach.b: If you see even your enemy's donkey collapsed under its load: "thou shalt surely release it with him." Help him, enemy or not, for the animal's sake.

"Thou shalt not muzzle the ox when he treadeth out the corn": let a working animal eat from what it's working on. On Shabbat, your ox and donkey rest too. If you take eggs from a nest, first send the mother bird away.
The Talmud even draws a mealtime rule from a verse in the Shema, which says God will give grass for your cattle, and then says you'll eat and be satisfied. Cattle first, then you.
So Jewish law says to feed your animals before you sit down to eat.

teach.h: HIS TENDER MERCIES ARE OVER ALL.
teach.b: It connects back to kosher food too: the traditional method of slaughter, shechita, is meant to be a single swift cut, and an animal that's badly injured or diseased isn't kosher.
Look back at the week: the head, the strap like a ring, who wears them, what kosher means, which animals, meat and milk, and now the animals' own suffering.

how: Jewish law forbids causing animals needless suffering; many Jews feed their animals before eating themselves, let working animals rest on Shabbat, and expect kosher slaughter to be a single swift cut.

animals offered as sacrifices at the Temple

games.q: what the Torah asks for animals — tap the pairs.

s: Jewish law allows any treatment of animals
tza'ar ba'alei chayim forbids causing them needless suffering.
the Talmud says to feed your animals before you eat
grass for your cattle comes first in the verse, then you eat.

games.q: you're Rabbi Judah's housekeeper, sweeping out a nest of baby weasels. the rabbi sees you. what does he say?
o: leave them alone: His tender mercies are over all His works.
games.why: he quotes the psalm and tells her to leave them. the Talmud says his suffering ended because he showed mercy.

practice: Picture an animal near you, a pet, a bird at the window, an insect you'd usually swat, a dog on the sidewalk, and notice it has a body like yours: it gets hungry, tired, scared.
Then choose one small kindness you could offer it: fresh water, a gentle hand, or simply letting it go out the window instead of squashing it.

wordCard.voice: Ba'alei chayim. Living creatures, the Hebrew phrase at the heart of the Jewish principle that you may not cause an animal needless pain.

orig.note: Hebrew: the suffering of living creatures.

carryVoice: Your line: animals feel too. Mercy for a calf, a weasel, an enemy's donkey. Until tomorrow.
